Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

Queue with workers processes jobs as they arrive. A job enters a queue, and available workers pick it up and execute it. This model responds immediately to demand. If traffic spikes, more jobs queue up and workers process them in order. You can add workers to handle increased load, and remove them during quiet periods. The tradeoff is complexity—you need to maintain the queue itself, handle retries, manage worker lifecycle, and debug distributed failures.

Scheduled batch runs execute on a fixed schedule, typically once per hour or day. A single process wakes up, processes all pending work in one pass, then sleeps until the next scheduled time. This model is simpler. You define a cron job and let it run. Resource usage is predictable since you know when the work happens. The tradeoff is latency—a job created just after a batch runs must wait until the next scheduled time, potentially hours.

Use a queue for work that benefits from low latency or unpredictable volume—sending notifications, processing uploads, handling user-triggered exports. Use scheduled batches for work with fixed deadlines or predictable volume—generating daily reports, purging old records, syncing external systems. Many systems use both, handling reactive tasks with a queue and bulk operations with batches.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

In a queue system, when a worker processes a job and it fails, the job can be retried automatically. Most queue systems let you set a maximum retry count—if a job fails five times, it moves to a dead letter queue for manual investigation. Failures are isolated to that single job; other work continues normally. You need monitoring to catch dead letters, but the rest of your system stays running.

In a scheduled batch system, a failure during the run can halt the entire process. If you're processing 10,000 records and the 5,000th fails, you must decide whether to resume from that point in the next window, skip the failed record, or retry the whole batch. This creates a choice between losing data and repeating work. Partial failures are harder to track, and a systemic bug means all pending work waits until the next scheduled window.

Add a recommendation for a small team.

Queue with workers processes jobs as they arrive. When a job enters the queue, available workers pick it up and execute it. This model responds immediately to demand. If traffic spikes, jobs queue up and workers process them in order. You can add workers to handle peak load and remove them during quiet periods. The tradeoff is complexity—you need to maintain the queue itself, handle retries, manage worker lifecycle, and debug distributed failures.

Scheduled batch runs execute on a fixed schedule, typically once an hour or daily. A single process wakes up, processes all pending work in one pass, then sleeps until the next window. This model is simpler. You define a cron schedule and let it run. Resource usage is predictable since you know when work happens. The tradeoff is latency—a job created just after a batch runs must wait until the next scheduled time, potentially hours.

Use a queue for work that needs low latency or has unpredictable volume: sending notifications, processing uploads, handling exports. Use scheduled batches for work with fixed deadlines or steady volume: generating daily reports, purging old data, syncing external systems. Many systems use both—queues for reactive tasks and batches for bulk operations.

In a queue system, when a worker fails to process a job, the job can be retried automatically. Most queue systems let you set a retry limit. If a job fails five times, it moves to a dead-letter queue for investigation. Failures affect only that single job. Other work continues normally. You need monitoring to catch dead-letter jobs, but your system stays operational.

In a scheduled batch system, a failure during the run can halt the entire process. If you're processing 10,000 records and the 5,000th fails, you must choose whether to resume from that point on the next run, skip the failed record, or retry the whole batch. This creates tension between losing data and repeating work. Partial failures are hard to track. A systemic bug means all pending work waits until the next scheduled window.

Start with scheduled batches. They're simpler to build and operate—one process doing one job, with no queue service to manage. Simplicity matters when your team is small. Add a queue only when specific work needs faster response. Most small teams find that a basic scheduled batch handles the majority of their background jobs, and they add a queue only when latency becomes a genuine constraint.

Queue with workers processes jobs as they arrive. When a job enters the queue, available workers pick it up and execute it immediately—this model responds to demand spikes by queuing extra jobs, which remaining workers process in order. You can scale workers up during peak traffic and down during quiet periods. Scheduled batch runs execute once an hour or daily. A single process wakes up, processes all pending work in one pass, then sleeps until the next window. This is simpler.

Use a queue for work needing low latency or unpredictable volume: sending notifications, processing uploads, handling exports. Use scheduled batches for work with fixed deadlines or steady volume: generating daily reports, purging old data, syncing external systems. Many systems use both—queues for reactive tasks and batches for bulk operations.

When a worker fails to process a queue job, most systems retry automatically up to a limit. If a job fails five times, it moves to a dead-letter queue for investigation. Failures are isolated. Other work continues. You need monitoring to catch dead-letter jobs, but your system stays operational.

In a scheduled batch, a failure during the run can halt everything. Processing 10,000 records, if the 5,000th fails, you must choose whether to resume from that point on the next run, skip the failed record, or retry the whole batch. This creates tension between losing data and repeating work. A systemic bug means all pending work waits until the next scheduled window.

Start with scheduled batches. They're simpler to build and operate—one process, one job, no queue service to manage. Simplicity matters for small teams. Add a queue only when specific work genuinely needs faster response. Most small teams find that a basic scheduled batch handles the majority of their background jobs, and they add a queue only when latency becomes a genuine constraint rather than a hypothetical concern.
